speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monieilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Old Age Assistance Act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps a
brief statement is required of me at the opening of this debate on' second reading of the Old Age Assistance Act. Most of what I could usefully say has already been given in my statement on the resolution. Hon. members will see that the bill itself requires little explanation. We are simply re-enacting section 3(1) of the Old Age Assistance Act, changing the references to the maximum amount of assistance payable so that in future it will be set at $55 monthly; and, at the same time, we are changing section 3(2) of the act to read 10 years instead of 20 years as every point where reference is made to residence requirements.
Finally, section 3(2) is being further changed to provide an increase in the allowable income ceilings by $120 yearly in the case of single recipients and $240 yearly in the case of married couples. For example, where an unmarried recipient was formerly allowed to have $840 a year, including assistance, he will now be allowed a total of $960 a year, made up as follows: $660 by way of asistance and $300 by way of outside income, after which his assistance is reduced by the amount of excess income.
Where a married couple was formerly allowed to have $1,380 a year, including assistance, they will now be allowed a total of $1,620 a year. This can be made up in one of two ways. If both man and wife are eligible for assistance they can receive as much as $1,320 a year by way of assistance and $300 by way of outside income. If only one member of the couple is eligible for assistance they can receive only $660 by way of assistance but they can have as much as $960 a year in outside income before there is any reduction in the amount of assistance payable.
In the case of a married couple one of whom is blind the income ceiling is even higher. Such a couple may receive as much as $1,980 a year in total income, including assistance. Where one member of the couple is on old age assistance and the other is on blindness allowance they can receive as much as $1,320 a year by way of benefit and have, in addition, as much as $660 a year in outside income.
If only one member of the couple is on old age assistance and the blind spouse is,


for some reason, not in receipt of benefit, the total amount of assistance payable is only $660 a year; but in such circumstances the outside allowable income can be as much as $1,320 a year without reduction of benefit.
The second section of the amending bill provides that the effective date shall be November 1, 1957, as far as the federal government is concerned. But each province will, of course, have to come to a decision to implement these changes in its own jurisdiction before they can actually become effective. Copies of the amending legislation were sent to the provinces on Friday, and new draft agreements are ready to go forward for their consideration as soon as approval is given to the bill itself. The provinces will, naturally, be the ones to determine the dates on which these payments will commence within their jurisdictions.
I am assuming in all my calculations that all the provinces and territories will wish to enter into new agreements and to make them effective from November 1, but, of course, at the moment I have not had time to receive official word from the provinces on this point. There will be no difficulty about giving effect to the agreements retroactively to November 1, even though they may not actually be signed before the end of the year or a little later.
As far as I know, there is only one province where an actual amendment to the provincial law itself is necessary: and even in such case it has been the practice in the past, if a province so desires, to enter into a new agreement subject to an undertaking by the province that it will, at the next session of its legislature, present the necessary amendments for retroactive application and approval.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE, RESIDENCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words regarding this act. I do not think there will be too much discussion about the amount of assistance to be granted under the act because we have already had a great deal of discussion during the debate on the resolution. As far as this group is concerned we are going to go along with those who vote for this bill despite the fact, as has already been expressed, we do not believe the amount of assistance under the act is sufficient to meet the needs of those who require it.
My sojourn in the provincial legislature of British Columbia brought me into close contact with the operation of this statute and many of the people who are subservient to the regulations passed under this act. Although the minister disclaimed any intention of saying anything at the present time about the regulations I think some comment should be made upon them because although no question exists as to the desirability of having such an act and while the regulations have

not stultified the intention of the act they have nevertheless definitely curtailed its real effect.
So far as I am concerned I am in agreement with the purpose of this amendment despite the obvious inadequacy of the proposal to raise the assistance from $46 to $55. Why do I say it is inadequate? The hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) in speaking the other day sought to justify the increase of $6 granted by the Liberal government earlier this year by pointing out that the sum of $6 represented a 15 per cent increase. I agree with the hon. member, Mr. Speaker. Figures do not lie but the trouble is that since the act was passed in 1951 the cost of living has risen by approximately 10 per cent. In light of the fact that the $6 represented a 15 per cent increase it appears on the face of it to have been a fairly generous increase but let us examine it a little more closely.
Under the legislation it is assumed that old age assistance was adequate in 1951; that is the only basis for assuming that the 15 per cent increase was generous. It must also be assumed that the $40 payment based on the 1949 consumer's price index was sufficient. I point out to you that that is not correct. The assistance was inadequate long before that. The purchasing power of the dollar in 1949 had been pared to the point here its purchasing power in terms of the 1935-39 cost of living index was approximately 52 cents and by September 1957 that had dropped to approximately 46 cents. In the light of these figures which can be verified by consulting the publication of the dominion bureau of statistics the $40 pension granted under the original act was entirely and hopelessly inadequate.
The factor that has helped the pensioners of British Columbia is that the supplementary allowance granted by the province amounts to $20 a month under a means test. The average payment is $19.12 to each pensioner over all classes of old age assistance recipients. I have every reason to believe that British Columbia will maintain the present supplementary payment thus bringing old age assistance in that province to $75 per month. It may be pointed out that in addition to this those in receipt of supplementary payments are also entitled to medical, dental, optical and hospital treatment. Thus it is evident that the goal of providing $100 per month to those who require old age assistance has already been reached as far as that province is concerned.
The objective of better treatment has not been lost sight of. Because of all the foregoing conditions, many of our elderly citizens 96698-49
Old Age Assistance Act cannot enjoy the comforts and pleasures to which their services to this country entitle them.
The present regulations under which the act is administered produce many hardships. For instance, take the case of a couple living say, in Manitoba; when the lady of that couple has reached the age of 64 we will assume that her husband passes away and the couple have children living in British Columbia. These children say to their mother "Look mother, there is no object in your staying alone in Manitoba, you might just as well come to British Columbia." So the lady goes. Now when she reaches the age of 65 she applies for old age assistance in British Columbia; she cannot get it because she has not been resident in British Columbia for three years. She then returns to Manitoba and applies there; she cannot get it in Manitoba either because she left that province before she was 65 years of age. The tragedy of this situation is that this lady will never get old age assistance under the present regulations because her initial application is held against her for the rest of her natural life. She could live to the age of Methuselah and she will never get this assistance under the present regulation.
Again take the case of an applicant who owns his or her own property. Five per cent of the assessed value of such property is deducted as income. The idea is that such people are not paying rent and the country does not intend to contribute to the establishment of an estate. That is the reason given for the regulations. The net result of course is that the 5 per cent simply raises the municipal taxes on that property. That is all that happens. It is all very well to say these people are not paying rent but the fact remains that they are paying taxes and those taxes, insurance and so forth are the basis of rent. Why add to that amount by adding 5 per cent of the assessed value?
Again if a person has beyond a certain amount in the bank or if they have an insurance policy that insurance policy must be surrendered and the income therefrom, plus any surplus in the bank, must be invested in a government of Canada annuity, the proceeds of which are regarded as income. It is entirely overlooked that these people who have such surplus in the bank and particularly such an insurance policy realize that without this protection, where there is a couple, one of them being left after the other has passed away, the one who is left has no insurance and will be without the wherewithal to give a decent burial to the deceased partner. Again there is no reason to believe that the people who have accumulated an amount during their lifetime did

Old Age Assistance Act not intend to spend it on the necessary comforts they hoped to have in their old age.
May I suggest to the government that they give our elderly citizens some consideration with respect to the matter of housing because that is an extremely important factor to the old age pensioner. I listened to my hon. friend from, I believe, somewhere in Toronto who spoke yesterday referring to the fact that they have a housing scheme in that city which provides bachelor quarters for old age pensioners at $35 per month. In view of the fact that Ontario does not pay any supplement may I point out that these people are getting only $55 per month and if they pay from this income the $35 a month for the shelter which they require, that will leave them a margin of only $20 per month upon which to live for the rest of that period. I submit that it is not a practical proposition to expect these people to live on $20 per month.
The suggestion has been made in my province that the federal government under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could make special provisions for these elderly people who wish to get together and establish a community of their own, more or less on the lines carried out in Rotterdam during the reconstruction of that city. They would then be in a position of having their own village-if you wish to call it that-or it could easily be done in the form of another type of community which they would themselves administer and look after. They would then have an interest in life and would be able to provide the housing they require. It could easily be arranged that the income of anyone participating in such a scheme would not be such that they would be occupying premises needed for those living on lower incomes.
Another suggestion I would like the government to consider is this. My friends over there have been advocating that the means test be removed from the recipients of old age assistance in the age group from 65-69. I am inclined to go along with that up to a point but I would like to see the Old Age Assistance Act and the Old Age Security Act combined into one act with a means test, but that means test to apply solely to the eligibility of the person concerned to pay income tax. That is to say if a person or a couple were required to pay income tax since their relative tax would be more than their exemptions of $2,500 in the case of persons over 65, then when they become eligible for old age security at 65, they would be subject to that means test only. This would do away with all these other inflictions upon the elderly citizens of our country and give them


a reasonable chance to enjoy the amenities which our productive system can provide.
We have been niggling and chiseling with respect to this question and the time has come to look at this problem-and it is a problem-from the point of view of our Christian civilization and our Christian approach to life. Let us look at this matter as a Christian community trying to do its best to look after the needs of those who have reached the point where they cannot meet their requirements themselves.
Governments and legislatures must change their policy and we must change this economic system of ours immediately. These things have got to be done as quickly as possible to strike the bonds of economic slavery from our people and give them freedom to live their lives in their own way wherever they wish to live them. We should give the hungry bread and the fruits of the earth will be theirs. I appeal to this government and this legislature in the name of the God to whom we here offer prayers every day to free the poor from slavery and want and feed the peoples of this earth lest they perish as a result of our neglect.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE, RESIDENCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the words I have to say on this matter are very few. I was very interested in the constructive remarks of the gentleman who has just resumed his seat. I think his comments bearing on the regulations with regard to old age pensions and old age assistance are worthy of note and they just point up the fact that these matters require our constant attention. Much of the administration of these acts are left in the hands of the provinces and we know that the applying of the means test and all the rest of it can be a very expensive operation. I think this house is to be congratulated on the fact that it is bringing down with such rapidity this social legislation. It may not be all that we had hoped for, but at any rate, the house has got down to work in a very short time. The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne has been interrupted to get the legislation through with commendable rapidity. We have had legislation concerning cash advances, old age security, old age assistance, assistance to the blind and pension increases for those who are totally disabled.
In looking at this legislation, I wonder if we do not find in it something that is the real cause of a great deal of difficulty across the whole of Canada today, and that is the matter of inflation. The reason that we have to increase these pensions and allowances is that people find they are

unable to make ends meet on these allowances. They are in a condition of dire necessity and some of the cases are very tragic. A person cannot possibly live in most of the communities in this dominion of ours on the $40 per month or even the $46 per month. Fundamentally there is a big problem facing the Canadian people and this legislation points it out. It is the matter of inflation. When and where are those people who are in control of things in this country going to meet the problem of inflation. We drew the attention of the government to these facts during the speech from the throne, but apparently they neglected to do anything about them.
What is troubling the people who are trying to produce? I know that so far as the prairies are concerned, and I believe it is true in the rest of Canada, the big problem people are meeting today is one of the rising cost of production. Each day the costs go up. Involved in this problem of social legislation is the problem of people trying to make ends meet, to keep their business going. The matter of inflation is too serious to be neglected for very long. The idea of putting a little patch here or there is not going to remedy the situation. A few years ago we were told in this house that the cause of inflation was too much money chasing too few goods. This was the story the minister of finance gave us; it was the story the critics gave us and it was accepted by the Canadian people. But today, we have a different situation. We have a supply of goods. There is no scarcity.

speechtext:
Thank you very much. I think even you, Mr. Speaker, would admit that inflation is the basic cause behind the need for these amendments. If we could do something about reducing the cost of living by 30 per cent, then we would be bringing this kind of social legislation to all the people of Canada. We are pleased to support the increases in pension for these people who find that because of the increased cost of living the money which they are receiving does not meet their needs. I hope the government, if it does not do anything about inflation, will be prepared to introduce a further amendment next year and then, if the cost of living continues to rise, will introduce another one in 1959.
It has been suggested that it might be a good idea to link the pensions with the cost of living index. We will support this measure, 96698-49J
Old Age Assistance Act and we will be glad to see it go through. It will help a number of people, but it will not help them for very long if we do not prevent inflation. I would suggest to the government that in the forthcoming dominion-provincial conference they look into this problem of having uniform regulations to cover all the people in these social assistance brackets. Something should be done towards providing equal treatment to all the people in all provinces. It is an unfortunate thing when, as the previous speaker mentioned, a person moves from one province to another and forfeits his right to this assistance. This is wrong. Surely while the provincial ministers are here at the conference, they could take a look at this social legislation.
People come under the Old Age Assistance Act because their income is too low or because, in many cases, their ability to earn has been curtailed by illness. These people do not voluntarily put themselves in this position. If one studies and works with these people for any length of time one finds that their greatest need is not necessarily money. They do not want a handout. They would like to make their contributions to society. If you can find some work for those who are partially crippled, find something for them to justify their existence so that they feel they are of some use in the world, then you will be doing a great deal more than merely providing them with the money upon which to live. I feel that, with that attitude, we can solve these problems. I feel our efforts should be directed towards enabling these people to help themselves and take part in the life of the community in which they live.
Modern industry all too soon casts on the ash heap the people who cannot keep up with the machinery as it is turning around. It is a sad thing that a man, while still in the vigour of life, finds himself out of work. Society will not have completed its task or its duty to these citizens who have given so much to this country until that part of the lives of our citizens is looked after as well as their physical needs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to associate myself with the others who have spoken in favour of the bill that is before us. We do not feel that $55 is sufficient to give to the people who come under this legislation their fair share, their rightful share, of the great resources of this country. We certainly do feel that such a move is necessary at this time because of the very drastic rise in the cost of living.
I want to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz) yesterday when he pointed out,

Old Age Assistance Act very ably I thought, the very serious impact that inflation and the rising cost of living have had and are still having on all of the government's welfare legislation, including the present measure. maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCE, RESIDENCE AND ALLOWABLE INCOME
speechtext:
We have a new minister. I am not arguing about that, but the reports that come out in the newspapers would not indicate there had been a new minister or any number of new ministers or even a change in the government. On this very question, I see in today's Toronto Globe and Mail a headline to the effect that we now, for the seventh month, have a rise in the cost of living index. It has reached a new peak.
While we have a new Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) who is apparently trying to do something for the people affected under this legislation to help compensate them in some way for this rise in cost of living, I think he might have some discussion with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and other members of the cabinet in order to see what can be done to protect the legislation that we are today passing.
Legislation has been brought forward to deal with increases in the old age security pension, blind pension, war veterans allowance, old age assistance and so on. However, it seems to me that in the field of welfare legislation there is one act which has obviously been by-passed by the present administration. In the days ahead I hope this omission may be rectified. I refer to the fact that there has been no announcement that there is to be a comparable and substantial increase in family allowances so that the purchasing power of the family allowance might be restored at least to the degree that it is being restored under the present legislation. I would suggest to the minister that there should be an increase


in the family allowance by 60 per cent, as compared with the value of family allowances when they were first enacted in this country in 1944. If that minimum thing were done, it would restore the purchasing power of 1944 and 1945 to today's family allowances.
There is one other suggestion I want to make with reference to the provisions of this bill. In this act we have, as we have in many other acts, something of cost-sharing with the provinces. While this provision is made contributory in many ways, I feel that the federal government contribution should always be the larger amount or should always be a substantial amount, so that all the provinces may be able to share in this type of legislation.
I was pleased to hear the minister say this afternoon, as I believe he did, that he felt it was likely that all of the provinces would be able to share in the increase provided for in this legislation and make it available to persons within their provinces. We have a new minister as the minister suggests. We have a great many new ministers. We have many new faces in this house. Speaking for myself, I can say quite honestly that it is a refreshing thing when I speak now to have what appear to be so many interested members. I think part of the reason for that situation is that the government at this time has not a great preponderance of members in the house such as we experienced for so many years. It seems to me that members on both sides of the house are today much more in tune with public opinion than they were in many years gone by. We in this group felt that we were advancing the things that the people of the country wanted but when we faced the government on the opposite side with such an overwhelming majority we found that in many instances, our pleas fell on deaf ears.
As to the progress being made in this session so far,-and I include the progress which is being made in this legislation now before us-it would seem to me that we are making more and better progress with the house divided as it now is than we have made in any other year since I first came here in 1945. I think the government is much more likely to listen to public opinion and to listen to members of the house when it is a minority government than it is when it has a preponderant majority. While certain people may feel most uncomfortable about the present balance of power amongst the various parties in the House of Commons, I would suggest that the balance prevailing in the house today works and that it is

getting results for the Canadian people in reference to the legislation that is now being discussed. It seems to me that there are persons who are extremely uncomfortable in this present situation and it seems to me that most, if not all, of them are supporters and members of the government.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to have a word to say with respect to the responsibility for fixing the regulations concerning the means test. I notice that under this legislation the allowable income for a single person is $960. For a married person and his spouse it is $1,620, and for a married person with a spouse who is blind, $1,980 a year. This means, of course, that these people are on a means test.
I should like to know who makes the regulations governing the means test. Is it done by agreement between this government and the provincial governments? If it is, then I think some of us have a small grievance in respect of the rigidity of these regulations, these restrictions under which the means test operates. For example, I noticed some time ago that on one of these forms a question was asked of some old people: how much have you had given to you in the form of vegetables? Now that is a tiny little thing. I know of a case where people did answer the question by saying: yes, we received a few sacks of potatoes. And yet that was considered as part of their income.
I took the matter up with the officials concerned and said I thought this was drawing the line pretty thinly, because these people had relatives who were farmers, and these farmers gave these people some vegetables. Farmers usually raise a lot of vegetables. They feed turnips to their hogs, and potatoes to their cows, and it is a very little thing for farmers to give vegetables to old people. And yet under this means test the question to which I have referred was asked.
I had another case brought to my attention where a young couple had a home in a village. They had that home for the purpose of returning to it after spending a busy day in town. They had a spare room in their house which they offered to their mother and when it came to analysing the income of that woman who was a widow it was
considered that the room was worth a certain amount of money and was taken into account as part of the over-all means test.
I recall another case where a widow in receipt of old age assistance decided that two could live cheaper than one and so when the opportunity presented itself she took in a lady school teacher as a boarder. She thought perhaps she could make a little bit of money that way although it was not her intention to overdo the matter, but when it came to the means test the modest amount she received was considered as part of her income. These instances are almost too infinitesimal to even bother about, yet this unfair practice exists.
I know of another case involving an elderly lady who was in receipt of old age assistance. It was her custom to visit her daughter on a farm during the busy season of the year in order to help out by baby sitting, washing dishes and that sort of thing. She was on the farm for several weeks each year and the officials wanted to consider that as part of something she received in the nature of free room and board which affected her overall circumstances.
I think that sort of thing is drawing the line too thin. When I have taken these cases up with the officials my answer has been, "Well, these are the regulations. We do not like to think we are picayune about these things but, you see, when the officials of the department come along and examine these cases and draw out the files and look them over they get after us if we do not administer the regulations properly." That is the story they tell me.
May I ask the minister who it is that makes these regulations and why do the regulations include such small things as those I have described? Surely a son can provide a room in which his mother can live without it affecting her pension under the means test. Surely vegetables and perhaps occasionally some groceries can be given to these people without it having this effect. What difference does it make? It is such a small matter it should surely make no difference at all. Who makes these regulations? Does the minister not think that at least in some instances the regulations governing the means test are pretty restrictive?

We all know that the board of transport commissioners exercises, to some extent, jurisdiction over this company. The board has control of rates, but has no control over services. In order to illustrate my point, Mr. Speaker, I want to mention a small community in my constituency about seven miles south of the very productive city of Trail. In this community there are approximately 30 potential telephone users. The people of this community then took up the matter with the public utilities commission of British Columbia and found out, because this company came under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners, the public utilities commission had no authority to issue any orders with respect to services to be provided or rates.
As the board of transport commissioners had no authority to order this company to

extend their services in any direction or to provide any services, I am sure it is obvious to everyone that there is a gap in the necessary controls that either the federal or the provincial government should have over a public utility which has a monopoly in the area concerned. In my opinion there should be some amendment to the powers of the board of transport commissioners in this case, in view of the fact that the company is incorporated under federal legislation, in order to provide them with the power to issue instructions with respect to services.
I admit that the company have made great improvements in the interior of British Columbia; they have improved the services; they have installed automatic telephones in many communities and have extended the services. But, in my opinion, when a small community such as that within seven miles of the city of Trail requires telephone service, and has required it for years, it should be granted to them, according to the controls that should be exercised by the board of transport commissioners. I cannot see why these companies should have the opportunity to skim the cream off the business, as it were, and to deny services to communities such as this one.
In this case the expense involved is a very small amount indeed. I mention this matter at this time because I promised the residents of the community of Casino to bring this matter to the attention of the house and to suggest that the house give it some consideration. I think I will get some support from other members from British Columbia. There must be other instances of similar denial of service by this company.
I am glad that the bill will be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I trust that we will have an opportunity to examine the officials of the company and to ask questions and that, before this bill returns to this house, I shall have some assurance that the community of Casino will be provided with telephone service by the British Columbia Telephone Company.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the explanation of this bill given by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) and in his recital of the history of this company. I recall going into the history of this company myself 20 years ago in the provincial legislature in British Columbia when the public utilities commission was first set up. I discovered that this utility, the second largest or perhaps it is the largest one-I am subject to correction- in the province was put outside the scope of the public utilities commission because of its federal charter, and I investigated the history which was extremely interesting at the time. I am not going to go into the details of it now, but I should like to support my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) in his contention that either the board of transport commissioners should be given power to order extensions of service where necessary and economically feasible or else some steps should be taken to return this company to the control of the provincial public utilities commission.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre paid some tribute to the way in which this company has been extending its services. I am not quite sure what some of my neighbours would think if they had heard him. Seven unfortunate neighbours of mine are obliged to share a telephone with a member of parliament and can get hardly any use from the phone at all because neither they nor I are able to get a single direct line. None are available and none have been available, and the company can give me no assurance that at any time in the foreseeable future am I going to get it. Perhaps the $250 million capitalization will enable them to save my neighbours from that embarrassment.
Mention was made by the hon. member for Kootenay West of the board of transport
Private Bills
commissioners' authority over this company. It may be of interest to the house to know that in March, 1953, the board of transport commissioners held a hearing on an application for rate increases by this company. That application was opposed by the provincial government of British Columbia and, I believe, some 60 municipal councils. In the course of presenting their case in opposition they cited certain practices of this company with regard to the purchase of equipment, and the contention was made that grossly inflated prices were paid by the British Columbia Telephone Company to affiliated companies in the United States for the equipment which was used in the services of the British Columbia Telephone Company.
They listed at that time the enormously complicated family tree of which the British Columbia Telephone Company is one small member. I am not going to attempt to trace it for you, Mr. Speaker, as it is far too complex. However, in consulting Moody's Annual I notice some rather astonishing figures with regard to some of the values of the present capitalization of this company. I am not sufficient of a financier to know exactly what type of shares are listed in Moody's Annual, but it shows some 10,000 preferential six per cent cumulative shares, on which in 1956 there was earned $480.25 a share of a par value of $100. In Moody's Annual I also found reference to the recent merger by which the British Columbia Telephone Company had now been joined to an even larger conglomeration of United States utility, finance and manufacturing companies.
After the board of transport commissioners, in March, 1953, held their hearing and cut down, in some respects, the application of the company for an increase in rates, an application was made by six citizens of British Columbia to the combines investigation branch on the basis of evidence that had been adduced before the board of transport commissioners. I understand that the hearing which was started by the combines investigation branch was not completed. Consequently there is no definite documentary evidence with regard to the investigations made. However, in the report of the director of investigation and research for the Combines Investigation Act for the fiscal year ended March, 1955, there is reference to the application which was received in July, 1953, from six citizens formally applying for investigation into the operations of the local telephone company and affiliated companies. While this report, in conformity with the regulations when an inquiry is not concluded, is extremely careful and there is no mention of the name of the company, it is purely an

assumption on my part, Mr. Speaker, that it must be the same company referred to.
I make that assumption because apparently the complaint was precisely on the grounds of the case presented by the government of British Columbia. At that time it was discovered that preliminary inquiry indicated that the purchasing procedures and company interrelationships described by the applicants were, as of the date of the application, or shortly prior thereto, substantially correct. That is to say, the telephone company purchased its supplies by private contracts through and from companies which were related to it by various intercompany stock holdings. The telephone company had a supply contract with a related company whereby the related company served the telephone company in the purchase of telephone equipment, the repair and rehabilitation of equipment, the assembly and installation of switchboard and central office equipment and the storage and warehousing of telephone equipment.
It also states in this preliminary report that while there was no specific evidence discovered of a combination to set prices in contravention of the Combines Investigation Act, it was nevertheless true that there was an agreement by these interrelated companies to supply equipment to their related company or child in British Columbia under noncompetitive rates; that is to say, they were going to make an agreement on their prices.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it may be that this company requires the extra capitalization that is called for, and certainly I would not wish to stand in the way of the British Columbia Telephone Company supplying a much more efficient and effective service than it has ever done in the past, supplying the communities which for 15 years have been demanding some care from this company, communities which were told at the end of the war that now that the war was over their requirements would be serviced. I would not want to stand in the way of this company doing that, but I would want to make sure that they are going to do it. I hope that when responsible officials of the company appear before the committee they will be prepared to answer some questions with regard to the interlocking relationship with United States corporations of whom the British Columbia Telephone Company is now a wholly owned subsidiary; that they will be prepared to- answer some searching questions as to the prices the telephone company pays for equipment compared with prices paid by other telephone companies to other manufacturing companies. If it does appear 
before the committee that the telephone company has been wasteful in the way of distributing its present returns, then some steps will be taken to see that in the future the people of British Columbia get the telephone service they are entitled to at the minimum cost without being obliged to pay tribute to companies which are outside the control of this parliament, the board of transport commissioners or any body set up by this parliament.

speechtext:
I would like to supplement in a few words what was said by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). I think the past has certainly demonstrated that this company in the province of British Columbia has not displayed that social conscience which should be part of a public service operation. I had the experience in the 1930's -I think it was 1936-of working for a crown company, the Dominion Telegraph Company, which was engaged at that time- although I was just carrying a pick and shovel-in resetting the telephone pole lines in the interior of British Columbia through centres such as Lytton, Lillooet, Bridge River, and 100 Miles. All I can remember about it now is that it was a very hard job; it was a 10-hour job in the hot, broiling sun of the British Columbia interior but I want to tell the house what happened. These lines were being operated by the Dominion Telegraph, at the expense of the country as a whole, as a loss operation, performing a useful public function. But as the population increased along those lines and businesses came in, as it got to the point where it was a profitable operation, of course, the British Columbia Telephone Company took it over. I do not think the parliament of Canada has any ownership or equity in those lines any longer.
I can see the point made by the hon. member for Kootenay West, that when there is really a public service operated under the dictates of private profit the public service is sacrificed to the needs of private profit and I can see the necessity, when you have something which is a public utility, of seeing that if they make profits in the rich areas such as the lower mainland of British Columbia, then they have a duty to operate, if necessary at a loss, to carry that service, when it is badly needed, in the rural areas.
I welcome the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) that this matter is to be referred to a standing committee of this house. I hope this point that has been brought out will be one of the things that will be dealt with by the

committee. I hope the committee will investigate as to whether or not the increased capitalization that is asked for can in some way be put on the market in such a fashion that Canadian people, and particularly British Columbia investors, can have, yes, control of that undertaking.
I agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) that it is a pity that one of our essential services in the province of British Columbia should be under remote control of a giant United States company, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, which, of course, has very little interest in service in the province of British Columbia.
I should like to know whether in the past, in the stock issues that have taken place, there has been any share-splitting or any stock dividend. I should like to know what assurance we shall have that in the future, if this increased capitalization is granted, it will not be bartered away in whole or in part in the form of stock dividends. Therefore, I appreciate the introductory remarks which have been made, Mr. Speaker, and hope that when the committee has investigated this matter further we shall be in a better position to judge the merits of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, when speaking on the debate on second reading my friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Jung) was perhaps just a little bit sketchy in dealing with this company because I think the house got the impression that this company was incorporated in 1916. Well now, a company was incorporated in 1916 by private act of the parliament of Canada, it is quite true, but it was not the British Columbia Telephone Company; rather, it was the Western Canada Telephone Company. In that statute there was provision for that company to change its name with the consent of the secretary of state for Canada to the British Columbia Telephone Company and there was also power given to that company to take

over the undertakings of a provincial company known as the British Columbia Telephone Company Limited.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, this company has a very long history when the length of civilization, you might say, in the Pacific province is considered because it starts with the incorporation in 1880 of a telephone company known as the Victoria and Esquimalt Telephone Company. Then there was a further telephone company established in 1884, the New Westminster and Port Moody Telephone Company which afterwards changed its name to the New Westminster and Burrard Inlet Telephone Company. There was also the Nanaimo Telephone Company established in 1892 and an incorporated company known as the Vernon and Nelson Telephone Company came into being in 1890. The latter company caused a little amusement in British Columbia because at that time the people on the coast wondered why the tea-drinking Englishmen who paid tribute to the time honoured custom of playing cricket and growing apples in Vernon wanted to talk to the hard-working, hard-drinking miners in Nelson; but anyway a company bearing that name was incorporated.
That company had extensive amendments made to its act of incorporation and by a process of absorption, after first changing its name to British Columbia Telephone Company, Limited, it drew in these various other smaller companies and at a long time prior to the passage of the Western Canada Telephone Company Act in 1916. I might say that this telephone operation, in 1916, was not a penny ante operation, it was a big one in the province of British Columbia. It had seen the ordinary development of the province. It had been through the boom we had in that province in its development prior to world war I, the development during the war years and the development in the roaring twenties, as they were called. It existed through the further development prior to the last war, during the years of the war and the development which occurred following world war II.
What puzzles me, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that in the whole period from 1880 on until now this very large operation got by with a capital of only $75 million. A long time has elapsed since then and there were several real boom periods which occurred in that period. As a matter of fact there are $13,-

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise in support of this bill. I have always been against speculation concerning the food of the nation which is one reason I wish to support it. I do not think there should be speculation at any time concerning the food of a nation.
When the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough) spoke a few days ago he referred to the fluctuation that had taken place on the market in rye and also in flax. If these commodities were under the wheat board such speculation would not be possible and fluctuation would be curbed.
It has always been the practice on the prairies for a farmer to pay his debts in October. In my 40 years in this country grain has always been cheaper in October than at any other time of the year. After it passes out of the hands of the farmer and into the grain trade the price begins to rise.
After the farmers got the wheat board we were able to get an average price for the things we had to sell, that is, in the way of grain. I think the wheat board has a lot to offer the farmer; it is not perfect by any means but it is better than anything we have ever had as far as giving the farmer a fair deal is concerned.
Now I notice that when we are talking about anything in connection with the wheat board or the grain exchange the hon. gentlemen in this house who in private life are lawyers get up. How ridiculous would it be for me to get up in a bar association meeting and tell them what I thought. I would never get near their organization to tell them what I thought about their business but they get up in this House of Commons and tell the farmers what to do. They belong to the


strongest union in the world, the lawyers' union; they can crucify a man, they can take away his bread and butter and still they have the audacity to get up and tell the farmer what he should do.
The farmer knows what he wants and if it were not for these lawyer fellows preaching about the grain exchange we would have got the things we wanted long ago. We have had two wars and what happened whenever we were at war? They took the grain away from the grain exchange and sat down and did things in a businesslike way; they could not afford to speculate then.
The troubles we have had in selling our crops have taken place since the Liverpool corn exchange was opened; while it was closed we had no trouble selling our grain, nation to nation, but now it is quite different. I do not want to hinder progress in this matter; I believe in the principle and I support the bill. I hope furthermore that the farmers in this country will also support it and let the lawyers go their own way.

speechtext:
Before the recess I expressed the hope that we would all work in unison for the complete abolition of the means test, wherever and however it applies. In my humble opinion the means test is not only unfair, it is downright unjust. The insistence upon a person being poor to get a pension and remaining poor to keep it is a subtle means to punish our good people who have worked and saved a few dollars or who have acquired property or who wish to supplement their meagre and insufficient pensions by continuing to earn a few dollars.
I have long felt that, age-wise at least, the most unfortunately placed people are those between 65 and 70 years of age. One of the main reasons for this is the iniquitous means test as it applies to them. They are forced to retire at 65, and more often than not on
a pension that is not only inadequate but which is just enough to prevent them from obtaining a government pension. They are unable to obtain work but are obliged to maintain the heavy expenses of keeping up a home. These good people are caught between the uncharitable, near-sighted and in some cases almost inhuman policies of industry on the one hand and the foolish and unnecessarily penalizing laws of government on the other. Sir, the pendulum has swung hard against our senior citizens. Wherever the means test reaches it wreaks havoc upon those who come under its yoke. I sincerely hope that this government will not fall into the same unfortunate attitude in regard to the means test as afflicted the late and unlamented government.
This afternoon I heard the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) speak about the means test. Why did he not, and why did not his late and happily deceased government recognize this problem? Why did they refuse to correct this unfortunate situation during the long, dreary and unproductive years they were in office? In so far as the blind people are concerned, the means test constitutes a particularly unjustifiable cross to be borne by people whose cross in life is already well nigh unsupportable. What strikes me as puerile and unjust in this measure, as in the previous similar measures with which I have dealt during the past two years, is the stark fact that here again we are insisting that a blind person be poor to receive the pension and stay poor to keep it.
Why do we not say to these people, here is an increase; good luck to you. If you can go out and, in spite of your handicap, supplement this pension by earning more, then so much the better. Let us give him our best wishes instead of this means test. Of course, coming from the maritimes as I do, I have long ago learned that half a loaf is better than none. In this case, the slice is so thin I can hardly see it. It is in this light that I approve of this measure as another faint step forward. In this case, let me assure you that I sincerely feel that this act, instead of reading as it does, should read that the means test has been abolished.

the second reading of Bill No. 23, to amend the Disabled Persons Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amending bill is a threefold one, as I indicated in my statement on the resolution. It raises the maximum monthly allowance to $55 if the provinces agree. It increases the over-all income ceiling by $120 in the case of single persons and $240 in the case of married persons. Both of these changes are the same as those we have debated and approved earlier today in connection with old age assistance. They have already been fully explained. There is, therefore, no need for me to discuss them more fully at this time.
The third change is designed to open the way for certain patients in infirmaries, homes for the aged and institutions for the care of incurables, to benefit for the first time from disability allowances. I gave a detailed explanation of the reasons for this proposed change in my statement on the resolution and hon. members will find that statement on page 683 of Hansard for November 1 last. I do not think there is any necessity for me to repeat those arguments at this time.
Reference was made in the course of the debate on the resolution to the need for a less restrictive definition of total and permanent disability than that which was in the regulations originally. Actually, as many hon. members who were in the former parliament will know, there was a change in the definition agreed upon with the provinces and made effective from July 1 of this year. This is a much simpler definition, the text of which is as follows:
For the purpose of the act and these regulations, a person shall be deemed to be totally and permanently disabled when suffering from a major physiological, anatomical or psychological impairment verified by objective medical findings which is likely to continue indefinitely without substantial improvement and, as a result thereof, such person is severely limited in activities pertaining to normal living.
Two meetings of the federal and provincial medical reviewing officers-all of them outstanding medical men in their own communities-have been held since disability allowances began on January 1, 1955. The purpose of these meetings has been to establish so far as may be possible common and uniform interpretations of various types and degrees of disability across this country. The most recent of these meetings was held on
Disabled Persons Act
June 25 of this year, to consider the application of the new definition which I have just quoted. It is my impression, Mr. Speaker, that we still have some distance to go before we can really say that we have established a satisfactory degree of uniformity in the application of this definition in the various provinces. But I can assure the house that we shall do our utmost in future to ensure that there is a fair, a reasonable and a uniform application and interpretation of this definition of total and permanent disability in all the provinces of Canada.
Meanwhile, I believe that I can give the house some tentative indications that the new and more generous definition of disability is having its effect. The net increase in the disability allowance case load in September was 1,272, the largest increase for any month since September, 1955. Only in five months since the disability program began, namely May tc September, 1955, when the program was just getting under way, have there been greater increases than in September of this year. Furthermore, the increase of 2,461 for the last quarter, July 1 to September 30, covering the period when the new definition has been in effect, was greater than that for the two preceding quarters put together, and greater than for any three month period since the end of December, 1955.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this provides pretty convincing evidence that the new definition adopted on July 1 of this year is having a beneficial effect. I suggest we should give it a try before deciding, perhaps prematurely, that it needs a further change.
A final word on costs. I will content myself here with repeating what I said in this connection at the resolution stage of the debate. We had at the end of September a case load of 35,490. With the effects of the new definition and the further changes now proposed we can estimate that this case load will rise and that it will average perhaps
43,000	or even more through the fiscal year 1958-59. The additional cost of the $9 monthly increase for this larger case load would therefore be in the neighbourhood of $4.5 to $5 million for a full year, with costs divided equally between the two levels of government.

I think most hon. members of this house have found that the definition of total and partial disability has been far too rigid. Instances have been brought to my attention of persons who are so disabled that they are completely unable to earn a livelihood for themselves and have become a burden to their relatives, but because of the very rigid definition of permanent and total disability they have not been able to receive benefit from the act.
I want to refer to the stand which the Saskatchewan government took on this particular matter on September 10 and to point out to the minister that this was during the month in which he said the largest number of additional persons could obtain benefit from the act, and to emphasize that even in this month when more people were coming under the provisions of this act, the feeling of the Saskatchewan government was that the definition should be further broadened. The premier has said that the Saskatchewan government has always felt that the old age assistance provisions were much too rigid and that they should be relaxed so as to provide an income under this act to persons who are unemployable, and that is the type of relaxation which the Saskatchewan government has in mind.
The minister has said that the door is not closed upon a further widening of this type of definition. I hope that in the near future there will be a further relaxation of these regulations. It seems to me that it is incongruous that a province which is short of revenue and which has always had difficulty in providing the revenues needed to carry out the undertakings in which it was engaged should have to go to the federal government

and ask that regulations be relaxed in order to bring more people under the act and, consequently, to increase in this instance the financial burden resting on that province. Mr. Speaker, I feel this is a progressive step but I am not altogether happy about the amount being increased to only $55 a month. I would have been much happier had it been $60 a month. With regard to this particular act, I would say that, strictly speaking, it is not a disabled persons act. In order to qualify under this act a person has to be 18 years of age and have resided in Canada for a period of 10 years and, moreover, I understand that such a person must be totally and permanently disabled. I say, therefore, that this act is limited in its application because it excludes a large number of people.
Sitting here and hearing about this amended definition which was given as of July 1, 1957, I wondered why there were not some other definitions in this particular act; for example, definitions covering partial permanent disability and also temporary total disability. I note that it is intended that there should be a proper interpretation of total and permanent disability, but the application of this act at the present time is limited to a certain type of individual who is totally and permanently disabled. It would seem that it may probably be expected that some time in the future this measure will be broadened so that it will provide greater coverage and include all those persons who suffer partial permanent disability and also temporary total disability. I trust that these matters will be considered by the government.

Mr. Chairman, in moving this resolution it again becomes very evident that veterans' legislation is never completed. Changes are always becoming necessary as times, situations and conditions change. I recall very well in 1946-47, as I am sure

War Veterans' Allowance Act many other members who were here at that time will remember, that when we passed what was known as the veterans' charter we thought we had pretty well completed veterans' legislation. Amendments have been made almost every year to the different acts that were considered and passed at that time. I feel it is only right and proper, at a time when the house is considering social legislation, that the War Veterans' Allowance Act should be given consideration.
This resolution forecasts legislation which is intended to, and which will help a most deserving group of our citizens. On different occasions I have said, and I repeat now, that I consider the War Veterans' Allowance Act one of the finest pieces of legislation ever passed by a Canadian parliament. I realize, Mr. Chairman, that at this stage it would not be proper for me to give full details of the proposed legislation. However, I am sure hon. members will wish me to indicate the main provisions in general terms.
The resolution now before the committee is consequent upon the announcement made in the speech from the throne that the War Veterans' Allowance Act, 1952, would be amended during the course of the present session. Hon. members will recall that this act was completely revised in 1952, and was amended in 1955. Furthermore, by means of a vote in the supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year, approved by the Appropriation Act No. 4, 1957, certain increases were made in the married rate of allowance and in the married and single rates of permissible income. Had the present government been satisfied with these increases, it would have been desirable anyway to have opened the War Veterans' Allowance Act at this session in order to incorporate the amendment in the act itself. However, as hon. members will see when the bill is in their hands, the government desires to go somewhat farther toward ameliorating the lot of those war veterans and widows who were trying to make ends meet on a small income.
The bill also reduces the period of qualifying residence in Canada of former members of the forces other than Canadian who were not domiciled in Canada prior to enlisting. It extends the eligibility under certain conditions to widows who are at present ineligible for the sole reason the husband died before completing his qualifying residence. Another amendment has to do with exempt income in respect of the recipient's home. The exempt value of such premises is raised.
Provision is made to remove from the act a clause which does not allow the award of supplementary allowances to an orphan in receipt of a pension under the Pensions Act.

The bill proposes to extend the period of absence from Canada which is permitted in any calendar year without loss of allowance. The bill also would extend eligibility for an allowance to a veteran of the Canadian forces who, during word war I, did not reach France but served in the United Kingdom for a specific minimum period.
Finally, the bill proposes an increase in the salary of the chairman and other members of the war veterans allowance board.
These salaries are set out in the statute itself and are felt by the government to be overdue for revision. I have tried, Mr. Chairman, to give hon. members a concise sketch of the amendments that the government has included in the bill to amend the War Veterans' Allowance Act, 1952. I shall, of course, be prepared to go into greater detail on the motion for second reading of the bill itself.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first words in the debate on this resolution, introduced by my old friend the present Minister for Veterans Affairs, would be to congratulate him upon attaining his present position. He has spent a great deal of time working for veterans ever since he was first elected to the house in 1935. I am sure the veterans of the country were quite pleased when there was to be a new veterans affairs minister from the party opposing that the appointment should have fallen to my hon. friend. I want to congratulate him upon attaining that position and to wish him success in serving the veterans of this country as his predecessors have done over the years since we have had such a ministry.
I should like, also, to commend the minister for the statement which he gave to The Legionary on attaining office. I thought it was in keeping with the attitude taken by ministers of veterans affairs of all parties ever since we have had a department of this nature. I should like to read to the house part of the statement the minister gave to The Legionary, which appears in the issue for August, 1957. He said:
Over the past 40 years Canada has evolved a veterans' charter which is broad in its scope and comprehensive in its provisions. It is our intention to administer the charter in the spirit in which it was conceived by parliament, and to keep in step, so far as possible, with the changing conditions of Canada's veterans and their dependants.
In carrying out our responsibilities to veterans and to Canada, we in the Department of Veterans Affairs will welcome the advice and assistance of all levels of the Canadian Legion. We hope that, in striving for our common goal, the welfare of our veterans, you will continue to co-operate with us wholeheartedly in the future as you have in the past.
The minister's comments in introducing the resolution were along the same line when

he referred, as he has done, to the working out of the veterans charter and the fact there was a real departure in procedure in that the government of the day referred the whole problem to a committee of veterans from all parties who worked out various bills which were then put before the government and, receiving their approval, were then brought into the house for second reading.
That veterans charter, as the minister has said, was regarded at the time as a great achievement, and as the new government enters on its task it would seem to me that it would be fair to take a look at the situation at the present time with regard to veterans problems as they are seen by the Canadian Legion. I have here what I think is a very good and very fair editorial which appeared in the August issue of The Legionary. I believe it reviews the situation as the veterans find it at the present time and, of course, the present government, as the minister has said, will feel that it is their duty to go on, probably in a less partisan way in this department than would be the case in any other, in consultation with the various veterans bodies to try to do a good job for veterans and their dependents. But before we go forward it seems to me it is quite fitting to examine the situation as we find it today. In many ways this editorial seems to me to be a very inspiring one to all of us who are faced with carrying on the work so well carried on in the past by those who dealt with this problem. The editorial is headed, "A Grand Tradition", and reads as follows:
While certain improvements are still being sought by the Canadian Legion and the new government will be urged to implement a number of Legion recommendations during the next session of parliament, it is a well established fact that Canada's veteran legislation is just about the best in the world. In some respects it is actually more generous than that of the United States, the wealthiest nation in existence, and in all aspects it is away ahead of the United Kingdom and every other nation. Not to bear this fact in mind would be both foolish and churlish.
Support of All Parties.
The principal reason for this singularly happy state of affairs is that, ever since the first world war, veteran legislation has been as close to being a non-party matter as any legislation can be which in the final analysis is the responsibility of the party and government in power. The various parliamentary committees on veterans affairs which over the years have dealt with proposed ex-service legislation have invariably been composed of war veteran members of all four parties in the House of Commons, and while the government has always had a majority in the committee in accordance with democratic practice it has only been on rare occasions that it has considered it necessary to use its majority vote. Practically all the committee recommendations, certainly all the major ones, have been unanimous.
D.V.A. Heads Through the Years.
By the same token the various cabinet ministers who have held the veterans affairs portfolio have been exceptionally free of political or party bias
War Veterans' Allowance Act in their handling of veteran legislation both in parliamentary committees and in the house as well as in their direction of the administration of the veterans charter by departmental officials. Like their M.P. comrade-in-arms in all parties, they have really had the welfare of their fellow veterans at heart and, within the limitations imposed by cabinet responsibility and solidarity, have done their utmost for those with whom they shared the dangers and hardships of war. Being in the pilot's seat, as it were, they have had a major share in guiding Canada's veteran legislation to its present position.
Canada's ex-servicemen and women will remember Sir James Lougheed, Dr. "Bob" Manion, Dr. H. Beland, Dr. J. H. King, Dr. Murray MacLaren, Donald Sutherland, C.G., "Chubby" Power, Ian Mackenzie, Milton Gregg, V.C. and "Bob" Lapointe primarily because they were their ministers of veterans affairs or of pensions and national health or of soldiers' civil reestablishment, to use the old titles by which some of the earlier ministers were known, not because they were members of this or that Conservative or Liberal government.
Defeated Ministers.
Only three of this distinguished company are still living-"Chubby" Power, who became Canada's dynamic air minister in the second world war and is now a member of the Senate; and Milton Gregg and Bob Lapointe who with seven of their cabinet colleagues went down to defeat in the recent general election. In so far as exservice legislation is concerned, these two will be missed in the new House of Commons. Under their respective regimes substantial benefits were granted disabled ex-servicemen and dependents, and both showed in their administration of D.V.A. and in their numerous dealings with the Canadian Legion that the wellbeing of their old comrades were uppermost in their hearts. Now that the turn of the political tide has removed them from participation in veterans affairs at the legislative level, it is only right and fair to say that they deserve the grateful thanks of Canada's exservicemen and women, and the best wishes for their future endeavours.
It is a grand thing that the tradition of veteran legislation on a non-party basis has grown up in this country. May it be jealously guarded and safely maintained by whatever party in in power!
As we have ended 22 years of Liberal administration in which this attitude was taken by the Liberal administration of the day towards working out and dealing with veterans problems whereby the co-operation and suggestions of members of all the other parties and of the people representing the various veterans organizations were sought and heeded to such an extent, I felt it would only be fair for me, inasmuch as I have watched this going on ever since 1935 and have been a member of committees for most of that period and worked with the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, to call this to mind and express my confidence, as he is so much in agreement with the course followed over the years when he took part in this work, that what is described in this fine editorial as a grand tradition will be carried on while he is the minister.
Nothing was said in the editorial about previous administrations, as a whole, but I felt that at this stage I should say a word or

War Veterans' Allowance Act two about such past administrations. Having had as much to do with veterans affairs as I did, in co-operation with the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie and other veteran members of the House of Commons in working out the veterans' charter, I felt I should say a word about the attitude of the government of the day and the ministers who had a great deal to do with the working out of the charter and the work that has been done since.
I think those who worked on that charter will agree with me that the attitude of the then prime minister, Mr. King, and the then minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, was one of very great sympathy towards working out the best charter for ex-servicemen that any country in the world could have.
At this stage I should like to pay tribute to the administration as a whole at that time and particularly to the minister of finance and the prime minister at that time for the way in which they were ready to accept advice from the veterans organizations and from the members of all parties in working out that charter. But, as the minister said, since that time there has been a period of 12 or 13 years in which great changes have come about in the country, and it was necessary to make great changes in the charter if it was to carry out the ideals and hopes of those who drew it. And so, carrying out in that grand tradition, members of all parties have been permitted, under the policy of the administration, led for over the past 10 years by the present Leader of the Opposition and with the co-operation of his administration, to carry on in that way and, as the Legion has said, accepting almost invariably unanimous recommendations of the committees on veterans affairs.
I was very interested in an editorial which appeared in the Torch, the voice of the Canadian corps. I will not take time to read all of it, but it has reference to this matter and it does pay a tribute to the present Leader of the Opposition who carried on this policy, it seems to me, in a way fully worthy of the great work that had been done before he took charge of the administration.
I do not think anyone would accuse the Canadian Corps Association of being biased in favour of our party. I was quite interested to see what they actually said and I really appreciate the generous and well deserved tribute that they paid. The editorial reads in part:
The Canadian Corps Association welcomes, sincerely, the new government elected in June of this year to guide the destiny of this great country of Canada. The new regime has taken over from the old which held power for many,

War Veterans' Allowance Act
I read that because I know it is sometimes suggested that the former administration decided on what should be done without listening enough to hon. members of the house or to representations in the country, and all that sort of thing. But actually, on the testimony in this regard of the present Minister of Agriculture, the government of that day invariably referred these matters to the veterans affairs committee and, as he pointed out in the speech I have referred to, the original idea that the government had in mind in 1947 was to raise pensions by 10 per cent, yet as a result of representations made by veterans organizations and the work of the veterans affairs committee, and consideration of the whole problem, the government finally agreed to raise the pension by 25 per cent.
After all, as everybody knows, the government at that time had a good majority in the house, yet here it was showing its attitude toward dealing with veterans affairs by not in any way taking advantage of its majority or insisting on having its own way. It listened to representations from the veterans affairs committee to the extent that it finally increased the pensions, not by 10 per cent as originally suggested but by 25 per cent.
Now I hope that this attitude taken by the former Liberal administration in not adhering in any stubborn way to any idea that it had in the face of representations made on behalf of veterans organizations and by people in parliament and in the country generally, will be borne in mind by the present occupants of the treasury benches for whatever time they remain where they are, and I hope it will also be borne in mind by the present minister with regard to the legislation which he is now bringing forward.
I am not in a position to speak at length about the proposed legislation because, as I have said, the minister has not given us much idea as to how far it is intended to go, but it seems to me that with the present fall in the value of money and the rise in the cost of living that this is, particularly, a time when the administration should be ready to call in the members of the other parties and deal with this matter in a committee where it will be possible to call in the representatives of the veterans organizations to discuss the government's recommendations and their adequacy in present circumstances. They have taken the attitude in the past that this is the right way to deal with this question. It seems to me it would be a very astonishing thing if they did not follow that course themselves.
