Mr. Chairman, I want to take this first opportunity to congratulate the minister on his appointment as Minister of Veterans Affairs. I must say that this is no mere formality on my part. I have had the opportunity and the pleasure of being a colleague of the minister on the committee of veterans affairs during the past 12 years whenever that committee was sitting, and one does not spend 12 years on a committee with a member in opposition without getting to know something about him and to appreciate him. I recognize the fact that the minister has good intentions and that he has always worked in the best interests of the veterans he has represented. I do hope that he brooks no interference from anyone when he is trying to give effect to the ideas which he has expressed during the last 12 years.
We in this group welcome this resolution and the proposals contained in it as outlined in the minister's opening remarks. I did not hear him any too clearly and I am not quite sure of some of the things he mentioned but in any event we in this group welcome the amendments as another step forward in improving the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
Although I listened very attentively while the minister spoke I thought there were some things omitted that the Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veterans have been advocating in recent years and I must deal with what the minister termed on July 16, 1956 as "some unfinished business". I can well remember his speech in this house on that occasion. Before proceeding further I must assure the minister that we in this group desire to co-operate. We will quote him and we will quote his colleagues but all we are doing is trying to co-operate in the effort he is putting forward to give effect to the ideas he has expressed during the last 12 years.
There is one serious proposal which has been made by the Canadian Legion this session which to date has not received a favourable response from the government and, of course, I refer to the suggestion that there should be a standing committee on veterans affairs. I am not suggesting we should expect everything to happen overnight and I realize that this session is carried on under somewhat unusual circumstances; possibly there is an atmosphere of the temporary surrounding the cabinet, but I do think, like the hon. member who preceded me, that even if a standing committee is not appointed this session this legislation should be referred to a special committee on veterans affairs, in

War Veterans' Allowance Act
compliance with the minister's proposals and wishes in years past, so the members of that committee will have the opportunity of hearing representations from veterans organizations.
I want to deal with a few matters of unfinished business so far as the veterans organizations are concerned. I understand that the Canadian Legion proposes that the ceilings on total permissible incomes under the War Veterans' Allowance Act be increased to $1,200 per year for the single recipient and $2,000 per year for the married recipient. If I understood him correctly I did not hear any mention of that in the minister's opening remarks.
The Legion is also anxious that the Canadian veterans of world war I whose overseas service was restricted to the United Kingdom be eligible for war veterans allowance provided that such service be at least one year in duration. If I heard the minister correctly I think something is being done to comply with that request of the Canadian Legion and the veterans organizations and, if so, I must say we in this group are very glad because these proposals have been brought before the veterans affairs committee and this house for a good number of years.
A third proposal of the Canadian Legion is that the widows of allied ex-servicemen be granted war veterans allowance in cases where the husband died before completing 20 years residence in Canada, provided:
(a)	that the effective date of her eligibility be 20 years after the husband's arrival to take up permanent residence in Canada;
(b)	that the widow herself has completed 20 years' residence in Canada, and (c) that the husband and wife were both otherwise eligible. Again if I heard the minister correctly I understand there is some move being made in that direction to implement this proposal and we are very pleased indeed.
The fourth proposal of the Canadian Legion is that section 8 of the War Veterans' Allowance Act be repealed. Section 8 of this act reads:
No allowance shall be paid in respect of any orphan who is in receipt of a pension under the Pension Act.
I understand that this section is unfair to the children of pensioners and in this case, too, I think I heard the minister suggest some amendment and we are pleased to hear that.
In addition to those proposals I want to suggest that there should be provision for the payment of the allowance outside Canada to veterans who have to leave this country for reasons of health. I know I raised this matter in the house on a number of occasions and I think other hon. members who were then in opposition supported it.
One particularly tragic case in my constituency comes to mind. A war veteran in receipt of the war veterans allowance was advised by his physician that because of an extremely unusual lung condition he would have to live in a very dry climate and suggested that he go to Mexico City. The veteran sold his little ranch, went to Mexico City and lived on a few hundred dollars for over a year. The people in my constituency sent him a little money to help him out because he was not permitted under the act to continue to receive his allowance outside Canada. This poor chap lived in Mexico City and after having spent his last dollar was found dead on the streets on December 31 last year.
My first intimation of this was a letter from a Mexican peasant who wrote and told me in very broken English what had happened. He explained that the chap had no money and his Mexican neighbours had taken up a collection amounting to 700 pesos and had provided for his funeral. This man wrote to ask if there could be some repayment of this money because they were extremely poor people. I hope the minister will introduce some amendment to prevent that sort of thing happening in the future. This was a veteran who had served overseas in the first war, lost his eldest son in the second war and suffered severe pains for years because of this lung condition which was not pensionable. He left the country and was denied the right of receiving his war veterans allowance.
In addition to that I want to make another suggestion with respect to an amendment I think should be made to the War Veterans' Allowance Act. Again it is a situation that has been brought to my attention in my own constituency and the person who suffers in this case is the widow of a man who served overseas in the first war. I am bringing it to the minister's attention particularly tonight because it would take such a small amendment to correct this situation. I urge an amendment to section 30 (11) (b) of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. This section of the act reads as follows:
A veteran who
(i)	is residing with a woman with whom he is prohibited from celebrating a marriage by reason of a previous marriage either of such woman or of himself with another person, and
(ii)	shows to the satisfaction of the district authority that he has, for seven years or more, continuously maintained and publicly represented such woman as his wife, shall be deemed to be married to that woman.
To illustrate the need for this small amendment to correct what I suppose are these very occasional injustices I want to relate this story. In October of 1914 a lady

War Veterans' Allowance Act was married in England but separated after six months and never saw her husband again. She learned, however, that he had ultimately enlisted in the British army but she never knew in what unit. In 1916 she heard that her husband had been killed but as she was not reported on his military service record as his wife and never, of course, received any separation allowance, she received no official notification of his death.
In 1918 the lady married a Canadian veteran in good faith and in the honest belief that she was a widow. They lived together from 1918 to May, 1956 a period of 38 years, until the death of this veteran. Long after her marriage this lady learned that her first husband had not been killed in France. I have known both these persons for many years and can say they are highly respected citizens of the community in which they live and are well known throughout the district. However, the war veterans allowance board cannot give the widow in question an allowance under the act because of the terms of section 30 (11) (b) because the veteran himself is dead and according to clause (ii) he must show to the satisfaction of the district authority that he has for seven years or more continuously maintained and publicly represented this woman as his wife.
I bring this to the minister's attention in the hope that he will give serious consideration to an amendment to the act to correct such a situation which I am sure would represent an extremely slight burden on the treasury because situations of this kind must be somewhat rare.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I see that my time is rapidly expiring owing to the verbosity of the colleague who preceded me. I must say that in view of the opinions expressed by the minister through the years and those of his colleagues, we certainly expect amendments in line with representations made by the Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veterans. I support the minister and his colleagues and, to inform his other colleagues in the cabinet what they stand for and what they believe in, I am just going to quote briefly from Hansard.
First of all I will quote the minister himself on July 6, 1956 at page 5751 of Hansard. He had this to say with respect to the ceiling on war veterans allowances:
I should like first to mention the ceiling on the war veterans' allowance. This is not new, Mr. Chairman; it is something which has been discussed at every veterans' meeting we have had in the past five or six years. As the minister pointed out, the ceiling on income for single veterans is $840; the ceiling on income for the married veteran is $1,440. The minister and other members, particularly the members of the veterans' committee will recall that the recommendation

which was made in 1952, I think it was, and repeated again in 1955, was that the ceiling should be $1,200 for single veterans and $2,000 for married veterans.	*
This was recommended to the committee after very serious study by Legion committees all across Canada. It was a great disappointment to veterans all across Canada when the government did not see fit at that time to raise the ceiling. It has worked a great hardship on the many individuals who are recipients of war veterans' allowances.
I do hope the minister will not continue to work a "great hardship" on the many veterans who are in receipt of war veterans allowances by failing to raise the ceiling.

And I would say the implication of the hon. gentleman's remarks is certainly that his attitude was favourable to the matter under discussion.
Now we have my old friend the Minister of Public Works. What does he have to say? On July 11, 1956 at page 5867 this is what the minister had to say and I will not quote at length:
The reason why he will not get it is because of the low ceiling placed on the annual income he is allowed. If that ceiling were raised from $840 per year to $1,200 per year for the single veteran, and from $1,440 per year to $2,000 per year for the married veteran, as requested year in and year out by the great veterans' organizations of this country, then that situation to which I have referred would be met. This veteran would be able to get his full old-age security payment when he reaches 70, and the small pensioner who is under 70 would be able to retain his small pension and get the full war veterans' allowance.
I support the minister in his proposal. Then we come to the Minister of Agriculture. Now he is on our side-he always has been- on page 5890 of Hansard on July 12, 1956 he says:
However, I would say I have never been able to understand why the government was not

willing at least to raise the amount of the permissive income. For many years past I have urged, as have others, that the limit on the permissive income should be increased to at least the amount of the income tax exemptions.
That would be $1,500 for a single man and $2,000 for a married man.
Now to conclude my quotations, which I am keeping very brief indeed, I want to quote the Prime Minister because he was really grandiloquent on this occasion. On July 12, 1956, I quote the present Prime Minister; at page 5897 of Hansard:
I should now like to say a word or two with reference to a matter that has been discussed on previous occasions, namely, war veterans allowances. As the situation is at the present time, the ceiling on income for the single veterans is $840 and for married veterans $1,440. I find it hard to understand why the amount should not be increased to the level of that amount which, under the Income Tax Act, becomes exempt from income taxation. This question has been asked the minister before: where is the sense of fairness in this situation? Everyone is entitled to the old age pension, whether it is the prime minister who receives it or somebody else. Every citizen in our country is entitled to it at 70 years of age. Why should those in receipt of war veterans allowance find the amount of their old age pensions in effect reduced on the achievement of the age of 70 years? That is something that one hears universally complained about. It is something that is unjust for, by reason of the present ceilings, it places those who served and their dependents in a second-class position with respect to others who did not serve. It brings about a state of affairs that is unfair and unjust and it constitutes a discrimination that cannot be justified. I ask the minister once more- as he has been asked on previous occasions-this question: Why should such a state of affairs be permitted to continue?
Then he goes on to say quite definitely:
Why has not the War Veterans' Allowance Act been amended so as to provide for payment of war veterans allowance to those who served in England during the first war?
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have made these quotations purely in a spirit of co-operation-
